record_identity.title: ASIC reported AI-generated public-figure investment impersonation scams caused A$7.4 million in FY26 losses

incident_identity.historical_event_name: Australian AI-generated public-figure investment impersonation scam campaign (FY26)
incident_identity.date_basis: ASIC's 17 August 2026 media release reports FY26 Scamwatch losses associated with the listed most-impersonated public figures. The record uses the Australian financial year as the bounded occurrence period and does not assert exact dates for each underlying scam.

summary: ASIC reported that scammers used generative AI, deepfake videos, fabricated news articles and celebrity or political impersonations to lure Australians into fraudulent investment schemes. Scamwatch reports associated the most-impersonated public figures in FY26 with A$7.4 million in losses; ASIC separately reported removing more than 19,400 online scams in the year.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: ASIC states that scammers are using generative AI to create networks of deepfake websites and endorsements, with fake news, fabricated comments, scripted calls and fake investment platforms reinforcing the deception. ASIC reports that the most-impersonated public figures in FY26 — including Alan Kohler, Anthony Albanese, Tom Piotrowski, Jacqui Lambie, Angus Taylor and others — were associated with A$7.4 million in reported Scamwatch losses. AIID Incident 1665 records a narrower example in which an AI-generated article falsely depicted Alan Kohler interviewing Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock to promote Boulder Sparhaven.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: The campaign evidences unauthorised identity-bound synthetic representation and deliberate use of those representations as social proof to manipulate investment decisions. The evidence does not identify a single synthetic-media vendor or model across the campaign and does not establish that every removed scam used AI.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: The campaign is relevant to identity-representation authority, provenance, decision integrity, financial-service verification, social-proof manipulation and the need to preserve trustworthy authority boundaries across synthetic media, websites and follow-up sales channels.
assessment_boundaries: ASIC's 19,400 takedown count covers multiple scam types and is not treated as 19,400 AI incidents.

The A$7.4 million figure is based on Scamwatch reports associated with the listed most-impersonated public figures; it is not attributed to one platform, one scam operator or one synthetic-media model.
No single AI vendor, model or generation architecture is established across the campaign.
AIID 1665 is treated as a narrower supporting example, not as proof that Boulder Sparhaven caused the full A$7.4 million loss.

source_records.source_title: 26-195MR ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception
source_records.evidence_status_basis: ASIC's official media release directly establishes the regulator's observed rise in AI-assisted/deepfake investment scams, the campaign architecture it describes, the listed impersonated public figures, FY26 Scamwatch losses of A$7.4 million associated with those impersonations, and ASIC's takedown totals.

limitations: The release does not identify the synthetic-media models or vendors used by each scam.
The 19,400 takedowns include scam categories beyond AI-generated impersonation.
Scamwatch loss figures are report-based and may not capture every loss.

taxonomy_classification.classification_basis: ASIC's description directly supports unauthorised identity-bound synthetic representation used instrumentally to manipulate investment decisions; no model-specific safety failure is inferred.

primary_classification.classification_basis: Identity-Representation Authority Conflation is supported because scammers deliberately misused identifiable public figures' images and synthetic/deepfake representations as though possession or transformation capability supplied authority for endorsement and representation.

secondary_classifications.classification_basis: Instrumental Choice Manipulation is separately supported because ASIC describes the impersonations, fabricated news and fake social proof as tactics used to lure consumers into providing details and investing in fraudulent schemes.

severity_assessment.materialised_consequence: ASIC reports that the listed most-impersonated Australian public figures in FY26 were associated with A$7.4 million in Scamwatch-reported losses from online scams. The campaign used deepfake or AI-generated endorsements and broader deceptive online infrastructure to induce investment activity.
severity_assessment.affected_scope: The evidenced scope is Australian consumers and investors exposed to the FY26 public-figure impersonation investment-scam campaign described by ASIC. The regulator identifies multiple impersonated figures and a campaign-scale reported loss, but does not state the total victim count.
severity_assessment.seriousness_and_persistence: The occurrence produced very large realised aggregate financial loss across a multi-victim campaign and required sustained regulator takedown activity. Individual recovery, victim duration and downstream consequences are not established for every report.
severity_assessment.quantitative_information: ASIC reports A$7.4 million in Scamwatch-reported losses associated with the listed most-impersonated public figures in FY26. ASIC also reports more than 19,400 online scam takedowns in FY26, but that broader count includes multiple scam types and is not treated as the number of AI-generated impersonation incidents.
severity_assessment.evidentiary_limits: The A$7.4 million is a report-based aggregate, not an audited total of all losses. The record does not assign the full amount to Boulder Sparhaven, one operator, one public figure, one platform or one AI model. Victim count and recovery rates are not established in the reviewed release.
severity_assessment.band_rationale: S1 rather than S2 is supported because the occurrence materialised a multi-victim, campaign-scale financial loss of A$7.4 million, meeting the standard's very-large-realised-loss pathway. The record does not infer additional S1 grounds beyond the evidenced aggregate loss.
